newsitem.title: USA: Silicon Graphics Q3 results underwhelm Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Silicon Graphics Q3 results underwhelm Wall Street.

text.p: Silicon Graphics Inc. Thursday reported operating earnings well below Wall Street expectations for its third quarter, adding to a series of consecutive earnings shortfalls.
After merger charges, the company reported third quarter net income of $11 million, or $0.06 a share, compared with net income of $52 million, or $0.31 per share, in the third quarter of fiscal 1996.
Even excluding the charges, net earnings per share per share were $0.09 a share, well below Wall Street's consensus estimate of $0.27 a share, according to First Call.

The earnings release was issued after the close, but traders said Silicon Graphics shares were changing hands in afterhours dealing for as low as $14 -- the lowest level for stock of the graphical computer maker since 1993.
"Where is the revenue and where are the earnings?" asked one agitated analyst after seeing the earnings report. "This is how many quarters in a row (of earnings disappointments)?"

Robert Herwick, who heads Herwick Capital Management, said investors who had bought into the company thinking the stock may have reached its trough "were kind of shocked," noting the company was still dealing with product transition issues.

Silicon Graphics (SGI) has been struggling for more than a year to regain its financial footing as it also absorbed the acquisition of supercomputing pioneer Cray Research Inc and launched a sweeping upgrade of its entire product line.

The company said revenues for the third quarter to March 31 were $909 million, up 15 percent from the pro forma $788 million combined SGI-Cray revenues a year ago and a 34 percent rise from SGI's own $677 million in the 1996 third quarter.
Shares of Silicon Graphics had already slipped to a 52-week low of $16.625 in trading ahead of the earnings release, before closing down $0.375 at $17 on Nasdaq.

Silicon Graphics CEO Edward McCracken said in a statement the company made "good progress" with its transition to the new "O Series" product line, but that its new high performance Octane desktop workstation had shipped in limited volume.

Herwick said the company's failure to get more of the new Octane products out the door at the end of the quarter, when it has historically been able to "frantically ship" to meet its numbers, was the "number one disappointment."
Gary Lauer, the company's executive vice president, said the company moved quickly to boost production of the Octane units when production began in the final eight days of March.
"It was the fastest manufacturing ramp (startup) in the history of our company," he said in an interview, saying the company had shipped over 1,100 Octane units to customers.
"We have now transitioned the entire product line -- the O series product line -- and we're in volume shipment across the product line, top to bottom," he said.

Lauer said Silicon Graphics' order backlog remains "very healthy" at $709 million, off somewhat after a quarter which tends to be seasonally weak, compared to a record $757 million at the end of December quarter.
"Bookings are in the range that we would expect on a seasonal basis," he added. At the end of 1996 product bookings had hit a record $955 million.

Silicon Graphics has been a pioneer in the area of computing-intensive graphics workstations, but faces increasing pressure from cheaper computer systems, including high-end PCs running on Intel Corp's microprocessors.
The company said the strong dollar also hurt revenue growth, along with weakness in parts of Europe and Asia, but Lauer said SGI's higher-end server sales were strong.

"Our high performance server business is growing at a very fast rate. It grew over 50 percent from the last quarter to this quarter sequentially and our server business is growing in the 90 percent range year over year," he said.

Lauer said its workstation unit shipments were up 65 percent compared to a year ago, and its low-end O2 workstation machines were growing "far in excess" of the 25 percent or so unit growth rate of machines running Microsoft's Windows NT.
In the next fiscal year, Lauer said, "There will be a much more concerted effort in our company, and there is today, on earnings growth and profitable growth."

"As we look to grow the revenues base of the company, we want to do it in a very profitable way. We think our earnings growth will be in excess of our revenue growth, that's our plan," said Lauer, who declined to elaborate.
